messages.subject: Producing plots for polishing in MS Powerpoint
parts:
Dear list,

Although I recognise the value of reproducible research, producing plots
in MS Excel or SigmaPlot, pasting and then ungrouping them in MS
Powerpoint, is the dominant technique for producing graphs for
publication in my area of expertise (agronomy). Tired of fighting
against the crowd, I'm looking for a way of doing this starting with a
ggplot2 graph; if you can't beat them, join them!

When if I do a plot in ggplot2, save it as wmf, and paste into a
Powerpoint slide I see that the smooth line and points have not its
original shape, but a serrated border as shown in the attached image.

# Do you obtain the same results with the example below?
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(x = seq(1, 10, by = 1), y = seq(1, 10, by = 1))
plot <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
geom_point() +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
theme_bw()
ggsave(plot, file = "plot.wmf", height = 10/2.54, width = 10/2.54)

parts:
Note that you can "fix" the image by ungrouping it and then editing the
points of the line. The line looks jagged because there are dozens of
points, and there should only be two (first and last). To do so, right-click
and select "Edit Points." To delete points, hold down control and click on
the middle points, leaving on the two endpoints.

You can see an example in the image attached.

It's likely to take 1-2 minutes per graph, though, which is a bit of a pain.

Although it may take some time to delete each point, it is good to know why the blue line was looking jagged. So thanks for the news!

Do you know why the black points (i.e. the geom_point) are looking jagged also? It seems that the problem disappear when you ungroup a plot whose point shapes are changed from 16 to 1 (see the attached or plot the code below):
df <- data.frame(x = seq(1, 10, by = 1), y = seq(1, 10, by = 1))

plot2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(shape = 1) +

geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw()

ggsave(plot2, file = "plot2.wmf", height = 10/2.54, width = 10/2.54)

Cheers,

Alan

Well, the plot you attached looks good when I ungroup it in PowerPoint. When I used the default solid points, those were actually not converted to circles, for whatever reason – but your hollow circles are. As a consequence, they looked jagged even when ungrouped.

 

I will note that WMF and EMF files are not anti-aliased in PowerPoint, but when you ungroup them (convert them to a drawing object) they are. So all WMF files will look jagged until they are ungrouped. Is that what you mean?

Alan

parts:
Alan

I have had a play around with your code and examples, trying different
formats etc and running through Inkscape, and can't find a good way of
getting this vector data into powerpoint. The plot lines persist in
being jagged, and this is a major issue, as the last thing you want do
be doing is editing the lines in the graph by hand - which points
should you delete? Each one will change the curve.

I'm also an agricultural scientist, and I don't know what it is about
agronomists and Powerpoint / Word etc, it's like there are no other
tools in the world. We have to put up with it, but don't need to
compromise completely!

Do you need to produce all of your plots in R? What about making
simple plots in Excel (export the data from R as a csv) so your
colleagues can play with it as much as they like. Excel can actually
be more efficient sometimes. Just make all the complicated ones in R.

For the complicated ones, I would simply produce two versions of each
plot - one with all the labels made in R, and one with just the plot
area and no labels or legends. Export them in a high-resolution raster
format so you know the lines are going to stay the same and nobody can
change those on you. The plot area can always be put into Powerpoint
and have whatever labels added over top.

If people want the plot area edited, offer to either do this for them
or send them the raw data in a .csv file so they can make it
themselves in Excel if they like (with a note along the lines of "I
made this in R because it is much faster than Excel for complicated
plots like this, and we do have a deadline on this project, but if you
have the time to reproduce it in Excel yourself you are most
welcome").

You'll waste days trying to get a vector export working to Powerpoint,
the results will never be that good, and your colleagues will end up
just thinking R is useless because you always send them ugly graphs.

Those are my outside-the-box thoughts anyway, I don't know if they are
helpful or not.

Samuel

parts:
Hi Samuel,

Sorry for the delay in replying and thanks for your comments. Of course
they are helpful.

Glad to know that I am not the only agricultural scientist wanting to
use different tools than Powerpoint and Excel!

I do all my graphs in ggplot2 and will not come back to Excel! So your
ideas about producing plots in R and then adding labels in PP are welcome.

Best regards,

Alan

> I have had a play around with your code and examples, trying different

> getting this vector data into powerpoint. The plot lines persist in
> being jagged, and this is a major issue, as the last thing you want do
> be doing is editing the lines in the graph by hand - which points
> should you delete? Each one will change the curve.
>
> I'm also an agricultural scientist, and I don't know what it is about
> agronomists and Powerpoint / Word etc, it's like there are no other
> tools in the world. We have to put up with it, but don't need to
> compromise completely!
>
> Do you need to produce all of your plots in R? What about making
> simple plots in Excel (export the data from R as a csv) so your
> colleagues can play with it as much as they like. Excel can actually
> be more efficient sometimes. Just make all the complicated ones in R.
>
> For the complicated ones, I would simply produce two versions of each
> plot - one with all the labels made in R, and one with just the plot
> area and no labels or legends. Export them in a high-resolution raster
> format so you know the lines are going to stay the same and nobody can
> change those on you. The plot area can always be put into Powerpoint
> and have whatever labels added over top.
>
> If people want the plot area edited, offer to either do this for them
> or send them the raw data in a .csv file so they can make it
> themselves in Excel if they like (with a note along the lines of "I
> made this in R because it is much faster than Excel for complicated
> plots like this, and we do have a deadline on this project, but if you
> have the time to reproduce it in Excel yourself you are most
> welcome").
>
> You'll waste days trying to get a vector export working to Powerpoint,
> the results will never be that good, and your colleagues will end up
> just thinking R is useless because you always send them ugly graphs.
>
> Those are my outside-the-box thoughts anyway, I don't know if they are
> helpful or not.
>
> Samuel
